title: Executive Assistant Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)
meta_description: A complete executive assistant resume example: calendar protection, multi-timezone travel, board preparation, and the exact bullet formula that turns trusted support into proof executives and applicant tracking systems both reward.
content_html:
Executive Assistant Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

An executive assistant resume has one job: prove you can be trusted with a leader’s time, travel, and information, not just that you can schedule meetings. Hiring executives do not hire for task lists, software inventories, or pleasant adjectives alone. They hire for calendars protected, trips untangled, board meetings delivered, and confidences kept: the responsibility you held, the action you took, and the result that followed.

Quick answer: An executive assistant resume should include a summary naming the level you supported and your strongest trust result, a skills section with calendar management, travel coordination, board preparation, and expense management, experience bullets pairing each responsibility with the time saved, trip delivered, or meeting prepared, and proof of discretion through duties handled, never secrets revealed.

Key Takeaways

  • Every experience bullet follows the same formula: responsibility + action + trust gained — the calendar you protected, the trip you untangled, the board meeting you delivered.
  • Lead with the level you supported and your headline trust result: EA to a CEO, a CFO, or a board, with travel across time zones, meetings prepared, or hours returned.
  • Spell tools exactly as postings do — Google Workspace, Microsoft Outlook, Concur, Slack, Asana — they are literal ATS keyword filters.
  • Show discretion through duties, never through secrets: name what you handled, never what it contained.
  • Keep the file itself single-column with standard headings and real text, so applicant tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Hiring Executives Actually Look For

Ask an executive what separates a keep-forever assistant from a risky one and it won’t be “highly organised.” It’ll be:

  • Calendars that hold. Priorities protected, conflicts resolved before they reach the executive, and focus time defended against the daily flood.
  • Travel that just works. Multi-timezone itineraries, last-minute changes rebooked quietly, and arrivals that never strand the traveller.
  • Meetings prepared, not just booked. Board packs assembled, briefings ready, attendees confirmed, and follow-ups chased without being asked.
  • Gatekeeping with judgment. Access granted and declined gracefully, inboxes triaged by importance, and interruptions filtered so only the real ones land.
  • Discretion that never leaks. Confidential matters handled as routine, private details never repeated, and trust earned by what is never said.

Executive Assistant Resume Example (Annotated)

Below is an example for an executive assistant supporting a chief executive and a board. It’s fictional — names and companies are illustrative — but every bullet follows the pattern hiring executives respond to: responsibility, action, trust gained.

ELENA VASQUEZ
Austin · (512) 555-0147 · elena.vasquez@email.com · linkedin.com/in/elenavasquez

SUMMARY
Executive assistant with 6 years supporting C-suite leaders, currently EA to the CEO of a 300-person SaaS company. Protect a calendar of 40+ meetings a week, coordinate travel across 12 time zones, prepare 4 board meetings a year, and return 10 hours a week to the CEO’s schedule. Known for calm under pressure and confidences kept.

SKILLS
Calendar management · Travel coordination · Board preparation · Inbox triage · Expense management · Google Workspace · Microsoft Outlook · Slack · Asana · Zoom · Concur · Event planning · Confidential correspondence

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Executive Assistant to the CEO — Northbeam Software, Austin | 2021–Present

  • Protect the CEO’s calendar across 40+ meetings a week: priorities defended, conflicts resolved before they surface, and 10 hours of focus time returned weekly.
  • Coordinate international travel across 12 time zones for the CEO and leadership team, rebooking disrupted itineraries within the hour so no meeting or investor visit is missed.
  • Prepare 4 board meetings a year end to end: board packs assembled, directors briefed, logistics confirmed, and follow-up actions tracked to completion.
  • Triage an inbox of 200+ messages a day, surfacing only what needs the CEO’s decision and resolving the rest independently, cutting response time on urgent matters to under 2 hours.
  • Manage confidential compensation and personnel correspondence for a 12-person leadership team, with no disclosure in 4 years of access.
  • Plan the annual leadership offsite for 60 attendees, from venue and travel to agenda and materials, delivered on budget with no scheduling conflicts.

Administrative Assistant — Halcyon Legal Group, Austin | 2018–2021

  • Supported 4 partners and their teams with scheduling, correspondence, and travel — the work that led into an executive assistant role.
  • Managed calendars for 4 partners, cutting double-bookings from weekly occurrences to none in a year by introducing a shared scheduling protocol.
  • Booked travel for 20 attorneys across 6 cities, reconciling expenses in Concur with zero late submissions in the final year.
  • Organised client meetings for up to 30 attendees, preparing rooms, materials, and agendas so partners walked in ready.

EDUCATION
BBA, Business Administration — 2018

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: level supported, tenure, and headline proof in three lines

The example opens with level and tenure, then the proof: meetings protected, travel untangled, board meetings delivered, hours returned. Without executive-level experience yet, lead with equivalent scope: “managed a 40-person office calendar and coordinated travel across 4 time zones for a regional director.”

Skills: tools and duties exactly as postings spell them

Executive support postings are keyword-dense, and applicant tracking systems screen for exact terms. Name your tools (Google Workspace, Microsoft Outlook, Concur) and your duties (calendar management, board preparation, expense management). “Great organiser” is not a keyword; “calendar management” is.

Experience: every bullet pairs a responsibility with the trust gained

The pattern is responsibility + action + result: “returned 10 hours a week by defending focus time”; “delivered 4 board meetings a year with no missed follow-ups.” Scope matters too — executives supported, meetings per week, time zones crossed, attendees coordinated.

Discretion: show it through duties, never through secrets

Every assistant claims discretion; the strong ones prove it by naming the duty and withholding the content: compensation matters handled, personnel correspondence managed, board materials prepared. One bullet about confidential work handled quietly proves the trust hiring executives pay for, and separates an executive assistant resume from a task list.

Executive Assistant Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting’s exact language and keep these groups on your resume:

  • Calendar & inbox: calendar management, scheduling, inbox triage, gatekeeping, prioritisation, meeting coordination (only the depth you genuinely have).
  • Travel & expenses: travel coordination, itinerary planning, expense management, Concur, visa and logistics support.
  • Meetings & boards: board preparation, agenda setting, minute taking, briefing materials, stakeholder liaison.
  • Tools: Google Workspace, Microsoft Outlook, Slack, Asana, Zoom, Concur, Microsoft Office.

Check your resume against a free ATS scan — for example, Cvyon's ATS grader — before you apply. Executive assistant resumes fail most often on vague bullets and missing keywords, not on formatting. Start from a clean template gallery or resume builder option, then verify with the free ATS grader.

5 Mistakes That Cost Executive Assistant Interviews

  1. Task lists instead of trust. “Scheduled meetings and booked travel” says nothing about the level you supported. Every bullet needs a responsibility, an action, and a trust gain.
  2. Secrets dressed as proof. Naming private figures, decisions, or individuals to sound important destroys the very trust the role requires. Name the duty, never the content.
  3. Vague support language. “Assisted executives” and “handled administration” mean nothing to a hiring executive. Name the level, the complexity, and the result: calendar protected, board meeting delivered, trip untangled.
  4. Tools without matching bullets. A software list proves nothing on its own. Pair each tool with work that used it: the calendar protected, the trip booked, the expense report reconciled.
  5. Unreadable formatting. Multi-column layouts, text boxes, and image-based PDFs scramble parsing, so your board-preparation section arrives as word soup. One column, standard headings, real text.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should be included in an executive assistant resume?

A summary naming the level you supported and your strongest trust result; a skills section with calendar management, travel coordination, board preparation, and expense management; experience bullets pairing each responsibility with the time saved, trip delivered, or meeting prepared; and proof of discretion through duties handled, never through secrets revealed. Trusted support beats task lists alone.

Do I need a degree to become an executive assistant?

Not always — executive assistants come from administrative support, office management, customer service, hospitality, and project coordination, and many enter through an administrative role plus a record of supporting senior leaders. Hiring executives weigh the level you supported and the complexity you handled far more than a specific degree. A degree helps for some employers, but a calendar protected, a board meeting delivered, and a crisis handled quietly prove more.

How do I show discretion on an executive assistant resume without revealing secrets?

Name the duty, never the content: “managed confidential compensation and personnel matters for a 12-person leadership team” proves discretion without disclosing anything private. Never name individuals, figures, or decisions that were not public. Recruiters read discretion as a skill: the duty stated plainly, the details withheld, and the trust implied by the level of access itself.

What is the difference between an executive assistant and an administrative assistant resume?

An administrative assistant resume proves reliable office support: scheduling, correspondence, supplies, and day-to-day coordination. An executive assistant resume proves judgment at executive level: protecting a leader’s calendar, untangling multi-timezone travel, preparing board materials, and gatekeeping access and information. The EA resume names the level supported and the complexity handled; the administrative resume names the tasks completed.

How do I write an executive assistant resume with no executive-level experience yet?

Lead with the closest equivalent work: calendars you managed, travel you booked, meetings you prepared, inboxes you triaged, or events you coordinated — then frame each as executive support in miniature. “Managed a 40-person office calendar and coordinated travel across 4 time zones for a regional director” proves the same skills at smaller scale. Add relevant software, run it through a free ATS grader first, and target chief-of-staff-adjacent or senior administrative roles as stepping stones.

Should an executive assistant resume list software tools?

Yes — tool keywords are literal ATS filters in executive support roles. List calendar and inbox tools (Google Workspace, Microsoft Outlook), travel and expense systems (Concur, Expensify), and coordination tools (Slack, Asana, Zoom) exactly as postings spell them, and only tools you genuinely use. A tool without a matching bullet reads thin, so pair each one with work that used it: the calendar protected, the trip booked, the expense report reconciled.
